title: APIs & Web Services
description: Designing APIs for many clients: GraphQL, gRPC, OAuth2, abuse protection and contracts.
resumo: GraphQL fits varied UIs; limit query depth and batch resolvers (no N+1). REST stays simpler for CRUD.
gRPC: binary Protobuf over HTTP/2 for internal traffic; never renumber fields — use `reserved`.
OAuth2 = delegated authorization (access tokens, scopes); OIDC = identity (ID token). Authorization Code + PKCE for apps.
The API accepts access tokens, never ID tokens.
Rate limit by API key or user (429 + Retry-After); behind a proxy, never by remote address.
Keep the OpenAPI spec in the repository and fail CI on breaking changes.

subsections.subtitle: GraphQL vs REST
subsections.description: Choosing by how the API is consumed.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** several apps and screens need different shapes of the same data, and the REST API either grows an endpoint per screen or returns too much.

**Concept:** GraphQL lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs in one call, solving over- and under-fetching for complex UIs with many screens and clients. In exchange, HTTP caching gets harder (everything is a POST to one endpoint), deep queries can be expensive (limit depth and complexity), and naive resolvers cause N+1 (use DataLoader or batching). REST stays simpler for CRUD and public APIs.

**How it works:** with Spring for GraphQL, `@QueryMapping` methods resolve the schema's queries, and `@BatchMapping` loads related data in batches.
examples.interview_question: When is GraphQL a better fit than REST?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: No limit on query depth. A client — or an attacker — can nest relationships many levels deep and make one request cost thousands of queries. Limit depth and complexity.

subsections.subtitle: gRPC and Streaming
subsections.description: Binary, typed contracts for fast service-to-service calls.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** internal services exchange millions of JSON messages per minute; serialization and HTTP/1.1 overhead become a real cost.

**Concept:** gRPC uses Protocol Buffers — binary, compact and strongly typed — over HTTP/2, with multiplexing and four call types: unary, server streaming, client streaming and bidirectional streaming. The `.proto` contract generates clients and servers in many languages.

**How it works:** use it for high-volume communication between internal services; for browsers and public APIs, REST and JSON remain more accessible.
examples.interview_question: When would you prefer gRPC to REST?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Changing or reusing field numbers. The number, not the name, identifies a field on the wire, so old clients read the new field as the old one. Never renumber; mark removed numbers as `reserved`.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a mobile app, a web app and partner systems must all call the API on behalf of users — without ever seeing their passwords.

**Concept:** OAuth2 is an authorization framework: it issues access tokens that let a client access resources on behalf of a user, limited by scopes. OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds authentication on top, with the ID token and the userinfo endpoint, saying who the user is. For web and mobile apps use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE; between services, Client Credentials.

**How it works:** short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens reduce the impact of a leak; scopes such as `orders:read` limit what each token can do.
examples.code:
# Authorization Code + PKCE (summary)
1. The app redirects: /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=app&scope=openid orders:read&code_challenge=...
2. The user signs in at the provider; the app receives ?code=abc
3. The app exchanges the code: POST /token (code + code_verifier)
4. It receives: access_token (short-lived), refresh_token, id_token (OIDC)
5. It calls the API: Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between OAuth2 and OIDC for an API?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Sending the ID token to the API. The ID token tells the client who logged in; it is not meant for the API, and its audience is the client, not the API. The API accepts access tokens.
examples.code:
# WRONG
Authorization: Bearer <id_token>

# RIGHT
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>      # audience = the API, with scopes

subsections.subtitle: Rate Limiting and Abuse Protection
subsections.formerSubtitle: Rate Limiting e Proteção contra Abuso
subsections.description: Keeping the API available for everyone.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** one client in a loop — or a bot — sends thousands of requests per second and the API slows down for everyone.

**Concept:** rate limiting caps requests per client (API key, user or IP) in a time window, usually with a token bucket. Over the limit, answer 429 Too Many Requests with `Retry-After`. Apply it in the API gateway or with a library such as Bucket4j, together with payload size limits, mandatory pagination and timeouts.

**How it works:** limit by the most specific identity you have: API key or user before IP.
examples.code:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
RateLimit-Limit: 100
RateLimit-Remaining: 0
RateLimit-Reset: 30

# Spring Cloud Gateway: limit per user with Redis
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: api
          uri: http://api-orders:8080
          predicates: ["Path=/api/**"]
          filters:
            - name: RequestRateLimiter
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 10
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 20
                key-resolver: "#{@userKeyResolver}"   # a KeyResolver bean that extracts the user
examples.interview_question: How do you protect a public API from abuse and traffic spikes?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Limiting by IP behind a load balancer or proxy. Every request then comes from the proxy's address, so all clients share one limit — or, if you trust `X-Forwarded-For` blindly, anyone can fake a new IP per request. Use the real client identity, and trust forwarded headers only from your own proxies.
examples.code:
# WRONG: the key is the remote address — behind the load balancer, it is always 10.0.0.5
key = request.getRemoteAddr()

# RIGHT: API key or authenticated user; IP only from trusted forwarded headers
key = apiKey != null ? apiKey : userId

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the frontend and the backend teams wait for each other, and a field renamed in the code quietly breaks the contract.

**Concept:** with code-first, springdoc-openapi generates the specification from controllers and annotations — quick to start. With contract-first, the OpenAPI file is written and reviewed first, and openapi-generator generates interfaces and clients, so frontend and backend can work in parallel.

**How it works:** either way, keep the specification in the repository and check in CI that changes are backward compatible.
examples.code:
<!-- pom.xml (code-first) -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
  <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
  <version>2.6.0</version>   <!-- springdoc 2.x for Spring Boot 3 -->
</dependency>
<!-- Swagger UI at /swagger-ui.html and the spec at /v3/api-docs -->

# contract-first: generate Spring interfaces from the spec
openapi-generator-cli generate -i api.yaml -g spring -o generated/
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between code-first and contract-first with OpenAPI?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: No breaking-change check. With code-first, renaming a field in a DTO changes the published contract silently, and clients find out in production. Compare the new spec with the released one in CI.
examples.code:
# WRONG: the spec changes with every refactor, nobody notices

# RIGHT: fail the pipeline on breaking changes
oasdiff breaking released/api.yaml target/api.yaml --fail-on ERR
